title: Multi-Agent AI for Production Security Operations: An A2A and MCP Architecture in a 5G Core
gist: A lead security architect documents a production multi-agent SOC running inside a Tier-1 telco's 5G core: narrow agents coordinated over A2A, environment access through MCP, LLM inference gated behind an Isolation Forest anomaly pre-filter, and a privileged reviewer agent whose safety constraints live in OPA policy code rather than in prompts, with Kyverno independently validating what reaches Kubernetes. Measured against the prior architecture it reports ~40% reductions in both MTTD and MTTR, more than 80 autonomously generated detection rules, and rule-authoring time compressed from about three hours to fifteen minutes — while explicitly rejecting both the monolithic-LLM and GenAI-on-SIEM patterns as dead ends at telco-core scale.

insights.claim: A multi-agent SOC architecture deployed in a Tier-1 telco's 5G core reduced mean time to detect and mean time to respond by approximately forty percent each against a baselined set of incident classes.
insights.speaker: Willem Berroubache
insights.so_what: One of the few published, operator-baselined efficacy numbers for production agentic security — the reference point buyers will benchmark vendor claims against.
insights.locator: Measured against a baselined set of incident classes

insights.claim: The system autonomously generated more than eighty detection rules that would not previously have been written, validated through the reviewer agent and human-spot-audited.
insights.speaker: Willem Berroubache
insights.so_what: Coverage growth, not analyst productivity, is the value the architecture actually delivers — a different ROI story than the assistant products most vendors sell.
insights.locator: has autonomously generated more than eighty detection rules

insights.claim: Human time required to produce a new detection rule fell roughly twelvefold, from about three hours to approximately fifteen minutes.
insights.speaker: Willem Berroubache
insights.so_what: A 12x compression on the scarcest resource in a SOC — detection engineering hours — is the concrete labour-productivity figure to model in security staffing plans.
insights.locator: Approximately twelve times the compression of human time

insights.claim: The author reports the platform monitors ten to twenty 5G network functions concurrently in the introduction but fifteen to twenty in the measured-outcomes section, an internal inconsistency in the reported scope.
insights.speaker: Willem Berroubache
insights.so_what: Scope figures in practitioner case studies drift; treat single-operator benchmarks as directional rather than precise when sizing comparable deployments.
insights.locator: The platform monitors ten to twenty 5G network functions

insights.claim: The figures come from the platform's internal benchmark and the operator's own incident-response metrics rather than a third-party study, and are baselined against the previous architecture at the same operator.
insights.speaker: Willem Berroubache
insights.so_what: Self-reported, single-baseline numbers cap how far these results generalise — an explicit caveat that most vendor case studies omit.
insights.quote: They are baselined against the previous architecture at the same operator; your baseline will look different.
insights.locator: The figures above need two pieces of context

themes.theme: Why the two dominant AI-SOC patterns fail

insights.claim: The real bottleneck in a mature SOC is rarely analyst triage but the detection-engineering team's ability to keep the rule base aligned with a threat landscape that evolves faster than rules can be written.
insights.speaker: Willem Berroubache
insights.so_what: Reframes where AI should be applied in security operations — tools that speed up triage attack the wrong constraint and will show weak ROI.
insights.quote: The bottleneck in a mature SOC is rarely analyst triage; rather, it is the detection-engineering team's ability to keep the rule base aligned with a threat landscape that evolves faster than rules can be written.
insights.locator: The problem you are about to face

insights.claim: Piping all telemetry into one large model fails for three compounding reasons: the context window is too small for real SOC telemetry breadth, the model is non-deterministic in ways unacceptable for outputs that trigger automated isolation on production infrastructure, and a single prompt edit changes the behaviour of the entire SOC.
insights.speaker: Willem Berroubache
insights.so_what: The change-management argument is the least discussed and most damaging — a monolithic prompt makes every SOC change a full-system regression risk.
insights.locator: The Monolithic LLM

insights.claim: Bolting GenAI onto a conventional SIEM/SOAR delivers analyst productivity gains but does not change the structural shape of the SOC, because rules remain hand-written and time-to-coverage on a new threat class is still bound by the detection team's writing speed.
insights.speaker: Willem Berroubache
insights.so_what: Directly challenges the dominant vendor roadmap — an LLM assistant on an existing SIEM is a productivity tool, not an architectural advance, and should be priced as such.
insights.quote: It delivers analyst productivity gains. It does not change the structural shape of the SOC.
insights.locator: GenAI Bolted Onto a Conventional SIEM/SOAR

insights.claim: The metric that should govern SOC architecture is the time between a new threat class appearing in the wild and the SOC having a deployed detection for it, not per-alert latency or analyst throughput.
insights.speaker: Willem Berroubache
insights.so_what: Changing the optimisation target changes the buying decision — tools should be evaluated on time-to-coverage, a metric almost no security vendor currently reports.
insights.quote: The metric that matters in a production Security Operations Center (SOC) is the time between a new threat class appearing in the wild and your SOC having a deployed detection for it.
insights.locator: Measure the right latency

themes.theme: Open protocols as the durability bet

insights.claim: Inter-agent traffic runs over A2A, which Google open-sourced in April 2025 and transferred to the Linux Foundation in June 2025, chosen over framework-specific buses because the useful life of a production multi-agent system is measured in years and coordination-layer durability dominates framework convenience.
insights.speaker: Willem Berroubache
insights.so_what: Protocol governance, not framework features, is the durable moat in agent infrastructure — a screen for which agent-tooling vendors survive a decade.
insights.quote: Open coordination and context protocols outlive frameworks; agents written eighteen months apart will still talk if they share A2A
insights.locator: Coordinate through an Agent-to-Agent (A2A) open protocol

insights.claim: MCP was donated by Anthropic to the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation in December 2025, and pairing it with A2A plus a CNCF substrate (Cilium, cert-manager, OPA, Kyverno, Argo CD, Prometheus) puts the whole stack under a single open governance umbrella.
insights.speaker: Willem Berroubache
insights.so_what: Single-umbrella open governance is itself a procurement and compliance argument in regulated industries — a non-technical reason regulated buyers will standardise on this stack.
insights.quote: The whole stack then sits under a single open governance umbrella, which is itself a procurement and compliance argument in regulated industries.
insights.locator: Property 2: Coordination Over an Open Protocol (A2A)

insights.claim: Routing every environment interaction through MCP servers means a new asset class or a replaced inventory system is absorbed by an MCP server's adapter with no agent prompt rewritten.
insights.speaker: Willem Berroubache
insights.so_what: Decoupling agent logic from tool churn is the mechanism that makes each newly exposed tool available to every agent at near-zero marginal integration cost.
insights.quote: When a new asset class is added or an inventory system is replaced, the change is absorbed by an MCP server's adapter; no agent prompt is rewritten.
insights.locator: Property 3: Environment integration over MCP

insights.claim: A2A task envelopes carry a trace_id that propagates so every downstream span — the detection agent's MCP call, the reviewer's policy evaluation, the eventual deployment — lives under one distributed trace, which is what makes the system debuggable.
insights.speaker: Willem Berroubache
insights.so_what: Distributed tracing across agent hops is the operational prerequisite for running multi-agent systems in production; systems without it cannot be incident-reviewed.
insights.quote: That is what makes the system debuggable.
insights.locator: Two things stand out. First, the agent-to-agent envelope carries a trace_id

insights.claim: A2A messages carry MCP URIs in a context_refs field rather than embedded context, so agents dereference at evaluation time — keeping payloads small, letting the context agent enforce access control at the MCP boundary, and making a single asset-inventory change immediately visible to every agent.
insights.speaker: Willem Berroubache
insights.so_what: Reference-passing rather than context-embedding is a concrete design pattern that simultaneously solves payload bloat, staleness, and authorisation in multi-agent systems.
insights.locator: Second, the context_refs field carries MCP URIs

insights.claim: Agent identity is a workload identity attached at the mesh layer (a spiffe:// identifier) and the MCP server enforces inventory authorisation on that identity rather than on any agent-supplied claim.
insights.speaker: Willem Berroubache
insights.so_what: Identity-as-traffic-policy pushes agent authorisation into existing service-mesh infrastructure instead of new agent-specific IAM, lowering the integration cost for cloud-native shops.
insights.quote: Identity-as-traffic-policy is the right place for it.
insights.locator: The agent's identity is a workload identity attached at the mesh layer

themes.theme: Safety as policy code, not prompts

insights.claim: No agent may initiate an externally visible action — deploying a detection rule, executing a containment, or modifying a firewall policy — without explicit approval from a privileged reviewer agent whose safety constraints are codified, version-controlled and independently testable.
insights.speaker: Willem Berroubache
insights.so_what: A single mandatory approval choke point is what makes autonomous action defensible to regulators in critical infrastructure; deployments without it should be treated as unsafe.
insights.quote: In a critical-infrastructure deployment, autonomous action is acceptable only because the reviewer makes it so.
insights.locator: Property 4: A Privileged Reviewer Agent

insights.claim: Encoding the reviewer's safety rules into a prompt and having the LLM reason about safety on the fly is identified as the specific mistake where most early multi-agent deployments fail; instead the reviewer calls a separate OPA policy layer and acts on a deterministic verdict while its own prompt stays short.
insights.speaker: Willem Berroubache
insights.so_what: Policy-as-code versus prompt-as-policy is the single sharpest diligence question to ask any agentic security vendor.
insights.quote: This is a bad idea. The reviewer agent calls out to a separate policy layer (in our case, OPA) and acts on a deterministic verdict
insights.locator: Because it is where most early multi-agent deployments fail

insights.claim: The safety stack is deliberately two independent layers: OPA enforces business safety invariants (blast radius, confidence, reversibility, escalation) while Kyverno independently validates at Kubernetes admission time how the action is expressed (trusted image sources, workload identity, resource constraints).
insights.speaker: Willem Berroubache
insights.so_what: Defence in depth between agent reasoning and production execution — Kyverno can reject a deployment even after the reviewer approved it, which is the property that makes the design auditable.
insights.quote: OPA enforces business safety invariants. Kyverno enforces platform security invariants.
insights.locator: What the Reviewer's Policy Actually Looks Like

insights.claim: Blast radius and confidence are estimated by the proposing agent, reversibility is derived from the action type, but config_validated is set only by the reviewer because an agent must not be able to mark its own configuration change as safe.
insights.speaker: Willem Berroubache
insights.so_what: Separating self-asserted fields from reviewer-asserted fields is the concrete mechanism preventing an agent from bootstrapping its own approval — directly copyable into any agent approval schema.
insights.quote: an agent should not be able to mark its own configuration change as safe
insights.locator: A quick note on the fields the OPA policy below relies on

insights.claim: Risk thresholds live in a separate data document rather than in the policy file, with published limits of 0.5 max blast radius and 0.7 min confidence for rule deployment, 0.2 and 0.9 for containment execution, and 0.3 and 0.8 for configuration changes.
insights.speaker: Willem Berroubache
insights.so_what: Published calibrated thresholds give other operators a starting point, and separating them from decision logic lets a SOC tighten risk tolerance without touching rule structure.
insights.locator: The thresholds themselves live in a separate data document

insights.claim: Kyverno policies catch a specific agent failure mode: an agent resolving a connectivity or access issue by widening a NetworkPolicy or ConfigMap until the symptom disappears, with an empty ingress from field silently meaning allow-everything.
insights.speaker: Willem Berroubache
insights.so_what: Over-permissive fixes are a predictable, testable agent behaviour — admission-time deny rules are the cheapest control against it.
insights.quote: A common failure mode when an agent is asked to resolve a connectivity or access issue is to widen a NetworkPolicy or a ConfigMap until the symptom disappears
insights.locator: The second code snippet is a rule that catches a different kind of mistake

insights.claim: Every consequential decision resolves to exactly three terminal states — auto-execute, auto-reject, or escalate to a SOC analyst with the full reasoning chain attached — with escalation triggered by low reviewer confidence, an always-escalate asset class, or an action exceeding configured blast radius.
insights.speaker: Willem Berroubache
insights.so_what: Making human escalation a normal protocol output rather than an exception path is the design detail that keeps human oversight functional under load.
insights.quote: Some decisions should never be automated.
insights.locator: Property 5: Human-in-the-Loop Is a First-Class Output

themes.theme: Anomaly-gated inference for cost and latency

insights.claim: Raw telemetry feature vectors are scored by an Isolation Forest trained on rolling historical traffic before any LLM is invoked, and only samples crossing a calibrated anomaly threshold are forwarded to the LLM-driven agents while everything else is summarised at the metric level and dropped.
insights.speaker: Willem Berroubache
insights.so_what: Putting a cheap classical model in front of expensive inference is the cost-control pattern that makes agentic AI viable at telco telemetry volumes — directly transferable to any high-volume AI pipeline.
insights.locator: The architecture solves this problem with anomaly-gated inference

insights.claim: Isolation Forest was chosen deliberately because it is fast at inference, requires no labelling, handles high-dimensional inputs well, and degrades gracefully under distribution drift.
insights.speaker: Willem Berroubache
insights.so_what: Four explicit selection criteria for a gating model, useful as a checklist when choosing pre-filters for other LLM pipelines.
insights.locator: Isolation Forest was chosen deliberately

insights.claim: With anomaly gating, per-event latency on the LLM path is bounded by the slowest agent in the fan-out and measured at low single-digit seconds end-to-end including reviewer policy evaluation.
insights.speaker: Willem Berroubache
insights.so_what: Concrete latency envelope showing multi-agent fan-out with policy evaluation is compatible with production security response times.
insights.locator: Per-event latency on the LLM path is bounded

insights.claim: The Isolation Forest is retrained weekly with feature drift between retrainings tracked as a first-class metric, because a stale anomaly model would silently widen the LLM's workload.
insights.speaker: Willem Berroubache
insights.so_what: Drift in the gating model shows up as an inference cost blowout rather than as a detection failure — a monitoring requirement most teams would miss.
insights.locator: The Isolation Forest is retrained weekly

insights.claim: The anomaly threshold is itself a policy parameter consulted by the reviewer, so under operational stress it can be tightened to reduce LLM load without redeploying any agent.
insights.speaker: Willem Berroubache
insights.so_what: Treating cost-control knobs as runtime policy rather than configuration constants gives operators a load-shedding lever during incidents.
insights.locator: The threshold is itself a policy parameter

insights.claim: The architecture uses five narrow agents — triage, detection engineering, response, context, and reviewer — each with a system prompt, tool list, output schema and escalation contract that fits on a single page.
insights.speaker: Willem Berroubache
insights.so_what: A page-length test for agent scope is an unusually concrete decomposition heuristic that can be applied in design review immediately.
insights.quote: If you cannot read an agent contract on one page, decompose the agent.
insights.locator: Property 1: Narrow Agents with Single-Page Contracts

insights.claim: The best-performing agents in evaluation had terse, job-description-like system prompts, and elaborate prompt personalities are characterised as technical debt that obscures the change-management story.
insights.speaker: Willem Berroubache
insights.so_what: Runs against prevailing prompt-engineering practice and implies prompt sophistication is a negative signal when auditing production agent systems.
insights.quote: cleverness in prompts is technical debt.
insights.locator: The temptation with large language models is to give agents

insights.claim: The response agent's actuator tools are read-only at proposal time, so an agent proposing containment cannot execute it before reviewer approval.
insights.speaker: Willem Berroubache
insights.so_what: Read-only-at-proposal is a simple tool-permission pattern that structurally prevents an agent from bypassing the approval gate.
insights.locator: Component Decomposition

insights.claim: The pattern fits only where the SOC is event-rich, the rule base is large enough that maintenance is a structural bottleneck, the cost of a missed detection is high, and the organisation has the engineering maturity to treat the reviewer's safety policy as a first-class artifact.
insights.speaker: Willem Berroubache
insights.so_what: A four-condition qualification test that disqualifies most enterprises, which caps the addressable market for this architecture to critical infrastructure, financial services and telco cores.
insights.locator: Trade-Offs and Limits of Applicability

insights.claim: The pattern is explicitly wrong where rule volumes are small, where regulation mandates fully deterministic statically-auditable detection logic, or where the operator lacks the engineering function to own the reviewer's safety policy — the last case being the most dangerous.
insights.speaker: Willem Berroubache
insights.so_what: The author states the platform is unsafe without policy ownership regardless of design quality, which is the disqualifier buyers should apply to themselves before purchasing.
insights.quote: Without that ownership, the platform is unsafe regardless of how well the rest is designed.
insights.locator: It is the wrong pattern if rule volumes are small

insights.claim: The architecture shifts detection engineers' work from rule authorship to reviewer-policy curation and agent-output audit but does not eliminate that work.
insights.speaker: Willem Berroubache
insights.so_what: Headcount savings do not materialise — the labour moves rather than disappears, which changes the business case from cost reduction to coverage expansion.
insights.locator: A few caveats are worth stating plainly

insights.claim: Because A2A and MCP are still evolving, any reviewer safety constraint that has not been red-teamed should be assumed insufficient.
insights.speaker: Willem Berroubache
insights.so_what: Red-teaming the policy layer, not just the model, becomes a recurring operating cost for anyone running agentic security in production.
insights.quote: A2A and MCP are still evolving, so any reviewer safety constraint that has not been red-teamed should be assumed insufficient.
insights.locator: A few caveats are worth stating plainly

insights.claim: In hindsight the author would split the single reviewer into a pre-execution reviewer that checks policy satisfaction and a post-execution auditor that verifies whether an action had the expected effect, with auditor findings feeding back into reviewer policy tuning.
insights.speaker: Willem Berroubache
insights.so_what: A closed feedback loop from outcomes to policy is the next architectural iteration to expect in agentic operations products.
insights.locator: What I Would Do Differently

insights.claim: The author underestimated the work of writing useful OPA policies — the code is small but designing the right invariants, especially blast-radius constraints, required several unbudgeted iterations with the SOC team.
insights.speaker: Willem Berroubache
insights.so_what: Policy design, not agent development, is the hidden cost line in agentic security projects and should be staffed explicitly in the plan.
insights.locator: I underestimated the work involved in writing useful OPA policies

insights.claim: Fanning events out to LLM-driven agents before adding the anomaly pre-filter created a cost and latency problem discovered only under production load, costing roughly a quarter of the project's operational firefighting.
insights.speaker: Willem Berroubache
insights.so_what: Inference cost problems in agent systems surface only at production volume — a reason to build gating in from day one rather than after a pilot.
insights.locator: Add the Anomaly as a Pre-Filter From Day One

insights.claim: The author predicts the field will converge on shared SOC-domain agent schemas in 2026-2027 and argues there is industry value in publishing reference schemas and opening the reviewer's policy language now.
insights.speaker: Willem Berroubache
insights.so_what: A named convergence window for domain-level agent standards — the layer above A2A/MCP where the next standards fight will happen.
insights.quote: The field will converge on shared schemas in 2026-2027; getting there sooner is better.
insights.locator: Publish the Schemas Earlier

insights.claim: The author argues the important work over the next eighteen months lies in hardening reviewer agents, standardising SOC-domain agent schemas and writing safety policies, not in scaling models.
insights.speaker: Willem Berroubache
insights.so_what: A practitioner at a Tier-1 telco locating the value in governance plumbing rather than model capability is a directional signal on where enterprise AI spend shifts next.
insights.quote: The interesting work for the next eighteen months will not be in scaling models.
insights.locator: Closing

insights.claim: The governing design discipline is to place cheaper, more predictable mechanisms in front of expensive ones, use open protocols rather than bespoke buses, put safety in policy-as-code rather than in system prompts, and make the human path a normal output rather than an exception bolted on.
insights.speaker: Willem Berroubache
insights.so_what: A four-line design doctrine that can be used directly as an evaluation rubric for any agentic production system.
insights.quote: Be disciplined about where you put the LLM, putting cheaper more predictable mechanisms in front of expensive ones.
insights.locator: Two questions I keep hearing since presenting this architecture at KubeCon
